WOLVERINE

BPC-157 + TB-500
Two of the community’s most popular recovery peptides. One combination whose reputation has developed much faster than its direct evidence.

“Wolverine” is the community nickname for combining BPC-157 and TB-500 around injury recovery, tissue repair and inflammation. Each component has its own research story. The combination itself is a different evidence question—and evidence from either ingredient cannot simply be added together and called evidence for the blend.

In Plain English

Wolverine combines BPC-157 and TB-500 in an attempt to bring together two different tissue-repair signals, which is why the blend has become so prominent in recovery communities.

Editorial verdict
Strong community signal.
Combination evidence is missing.

The rationale comes from two separate biological stories. Direct evidence that the combination improves human recovery is not established.

For blends, the Index separates evidence for the finished combination from evidence for its individual components.
01 / WHAT IT IS

A community-created recovery stack—not a single drug.

Wolverine is an informal name for using BPC-157 and TB-500 together. It is not a clinical term and does not describe an FDA-approved combination product.

The pairing is now sufficiently prominent that it appears in contemporary reporting and FDA adverse-event review materials. But popularity answers a different question from efficacy: it tells us what people are trying, not whether the combination has been shown to work.

02 / WHY THESE ARE COMBINED

The rationale is complementary repair biology.

BPC-157A 15-amino-acid peptide with extensive animal research around tissue repair, angiogenesis, inflammation and GI biology—but extremely limited human evidence.
TB-500A seven-amino-acid fragment related to thymosin beta-4. Its proposed repair rationale centers on actin/cell-migration biology, but human evidence for the TB-500 fragment itself is absent.
The combinationThe community hypothesis is that the two mechanisms may complement one another. That “synergy” is a hypothesis; it has not been established by a controlled combination study.
The evidence-transfer problem: research on BPC-157 does not prove TB-500 works, research on full-length thymosin beta-4 does not automatically prove TB-500 works, and evidence for either ingredient does not prove the two work better together.
03 / COMBINATION EVIDENCE

This is where the evidence becomes unusually thin.

We did not identify a controlled human trial testing BPC-157 + TB-500 as a combination therapy.

FDA's 2026 TB-500 review reported that its FAERS search found two cases involving “blended TB-500 and BPC-157,” but those reports did not contain safety assessments. FDA also stated that it had not identified clinical studies or human exposure data for TB-500 itself via any route.

That makes Wolverine a useful example of why the Index needs a separate Blend category: a combination can become culturally established long before the combination itself becomes scientifically established.

04 / COMPONENT EVIDENCE

Even the two ingredients do not have equivalent evidence.

BPC-157: the literature is dominated by animal and mechanistic research. A 2025 human IV pilot included only two participants and assessed short-term safety—not injury-repair efficacy.

TB-500: this is the seven-amino-acid N-acetyl-LKKTETQ fragment of thymosin beta-4. Human trials frequently cited in peptide discussions have studied full-length thymosin beta-4 rather than TB-500, and those molecules should not be treated as clinically interchangeable.

Blend rule: the weakest evidence link matters. A combination does not inherit the strongest evidence attached to whichever component—or related molecule—has the best research.
05 / COMMUNITY SIGNAL

This is exactly why Community Signal exists.

Wolverine has become one of the recognizable recovery combinations in peptide culture, particularly around musculoskeletal injuries, training recovery and post-injury experimentation.

That level of adoption is information. It can reveal where people believe they are seeing repeatable patterns and can help define questions worth studying. It does not tell us the size of an effect, whether the effect exceeds placebo or natural recovery, or whether the combination is safer or more effective than either component alone.

Clinical Evidence tells us what has been demonstrated. Community Signal tells us what may be emerging. The Gap tells us what still needs to be answered.
06 / CLAIM VS EVIDENCE

Where combination logic becomes combination mythology.

“Wolverine combines BPC-157 and TB-500.”Yes. That is the common contemporary use of the nickname.
“The two peptides work synergistically.”Plausible hypothesis, not demonstrated clinical fact. Direct controlled combination evidence is lacking.
“Both components have human healing trials.”No. BPC-157 human evidence is extremely limited, and FDA says it has not identified human exposure data for the TB-500 fragment.
“Human thymosin beta-4 studies validate TB-500.”No. Full-length thymosin beta-4 and the seven-amino-acid TB-500 fragment are related but distinct molecules.
“The blend is FDA approved.”No. Neither BPC-157 nor TB-500 is an FDA-approved drug, and Wolverine is not an FDA-approved combination therapy.
07 / THE GAP

VERY WIDE

Clinical Evidence × Community Signal
VERY WIDE

Wolverine has unusually strong community recognition relative to its direct evidence. The combination is built on plausible but separately derived repair biology; whether combining the compounds improves meaningful human recovery outcomes remains unanswered.

08 / SAFETY + REGULATORY

Combination uncertainty compounds component uncertainty.

FDA's current compounding safety information identifies potential immunogenicity and peptide-impurity/API-characterization concerns for BPC-157 and TB-500. For TB-500, FDA says it has not identified human exposure data and lacks important safety information.

At its July 2026 Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee meeting, FDA reviewed BPC-157-related and TB-500-related bulk substances for possible inclusion on the 503A Bulks List. That process concerns compounding policy; it is not FDA approval of either substance or of the Wolverine combination.

Combination-specific safety is another open question. Knowing the safety profile of individual ingredients—even if it were well characterized—would not by itself establish the safety of a combined formulation.
